questions.prompt: Complete: "Yesterday I ___ my grandparents in Sfax."
questions.explanation: "Yesterday" is an indicator of the past: the visit is a completed action, so we use the simple past — visited. "visit" is present; "have visited" (present perfect) never goes with a finished time like yesterday; "was visiting" describes an action in progress at a moment, not a completed visit.

options.text: I see this film last week.
I have seen this film last week.
I have saw this film last week.
I saw this film last week.

questions.explanation: "last week" is a finished time, so we use the simple past of the irregular verb "see": I saw this film last week. The present perfect ("have seen") never goes with a finished time; "have saw" also puts the simple past after have, where the participle "seen" is needed; "I see" is present.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct negative: "They ___ the homework on time."
questions.explanation: In the simple past negative, "did" carries the tense and the main verb goes back to its base form: didn't finish. "didn't finished" marks the past twice; "don't finish" is present; "wasn't finish" mixes "be" with a base verb (and "they" would need were).

questions.prompt: Complete: "___ you ever ___ in a hotel?"
questions.explanation: "ever" asks about an experience, so we use the present perfect: Have + subject + ever + past participle — Have you ever stayed in a hotel? "you" takes have, not has; after have the verb takes its past participle (stayed), never the base form (stay) or the -ing form (staying).

The past progressive is was/were + verb + ing, and "you" always takes "were", even for one person: You were helping your friend. "You was helping" breaks this agreement; "were help" forgets the -ing; "You helping" forgets was/were.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct pair: "Our town ___ a lot lately. Ten years ago, it ___ very small."
questions.explanation: "lately" goes with the present perfect, and this is a change between the past and now: Our town has changed a lot lately. ✓ "Ten years ago" is a finished time, so the second verb is simple past: it was very small. The trap is to keep one tense for both sentences: "has been" cannot go with "ten years ago", and "changed" does not go with "lately".
